To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

sleep has been neglected in sociology; it is an important element of consumer culture and the consumer identities and lifestyles that it spawns; it is increasingly recognised as a performance enhancer in the workplace, as a stress-reliever, and as a means to health and beauty; and, it is a crucial part of consumption, augmentating existing theoretical and empirical work in sociology.
sleep, as an under-researched and under-theorized aspect of social life, has become increasingly significant as an object of consumer culture.

the sociology of consumption has neglected the matter of sleep and its relationship with consumption, that this is a significant oversight, that sleep has a variety of relationships with consumer culture, including the ‘sleep industry’, and that these relationships are significant in their own right and in their broader sociological implications.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which sleep and sleeping are represented and experienced in contemporary society, and how these representations are changing in response to wider social changes.
the following questions: What does it mean to sleep in a culture of consumption?
the following: the ways in which sleep is consumed, the ways in which it is consumed and how consumption is implicated in the ways that sleep is consumed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
sleep is a crucial element in consumer culture, and the sociology of consumption in particular.
sleep, as a sociological object, is not just about sleep.
sleep is an important element in the consumption process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are all sleepers in the sense that we are all consumers of sleep, and that we are all consumed by sleep in the sense that it is an integral element of the consumer culture we live in. ‘Consumed with sleep?
the paper is about how sleep is being used to enhance the consumer experience.
sleep is not just a ‘social fact’, but a ‘social force’.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sleep matters in consumer culture.
we are ‘consumed with sleep’.

the sociology of consumption needs to pay more attention to sleep and the role it plays in consumer culture, and that the sociology of sleep needs to pay attention to the role of consumption in the social production of sleep.
